ing: cut in short lengths, or green onions
st: Soak the rice noodles in warm tap water until bendy but still firm, then drain well.
Stir together the fish sauce, tamarind and sugar in a small bowl until the sugar dissolves. This is your sauce.
Heat [[2 tbsp]] oil in a large wok or skillet over high heat. Fry the shallot, garlic and tofu for 1 minute.
Add the shrimp and cook until just pink, about 2 minutes. Push everything to one side.
Add [[1 tbsp]] oil and crack the eggs into the empty space. Scramble until nearly set.
Add the drained noodles and the sauce. Toss constantly until the noodles are soft and have absorbed the sauce, adding a splash of water if they seem dry.
Add [[1 cup]] bean sprouts, the chives and half the peanuts, and toss for 30 seconds.
Serve on plates topped with the remaining peanuts and [[0.5 cup]] raw bean sprouts, with lime wedges and chili flakes.
Peel the shrimp and keep the shells. Devein the shrimp and set aside.
Bring [[5 cups]] water or stock to a boil. Add the shrimp shells and simmer for 10 minutes for flavor, then strain and return the liquid to the pot.
Add the lemongrass, galangal, lime leaves, shallots and chilies to the liquid and simmer.
Add the mushrooms and cook until just tender.
Stir in the chili paste if using, then add the shrimp. Cook until they turn pink and curl, about 3 minutes.
Turn off the heat. Stir in the fish sauce and lime juice.
Taste and balance: it should be hot, sour and salty. Add more lime or fish sauce if needed.
Serve with cilantro on top. Do not eat the lemongrass, galangal or leaves.
Pour the stock and [[1 cup]] of the coconut milk into a pot. Bring to a gentle simmer; do not boil hard or it may separate.
Add the galangal, lemongrass, lime leaves and chilies. Simmer to infuse the broth.
Add the chicken and mushrooms and cook until the chicken is white all through.
Pour in the remaining [[1 cup]] coconut milk and warm it through.
Check that the chicken is cooked to 165°F (74°C).
Take off the heat and stir in the fish sauce, sugar and lime juice.
Taste and adjust; it should be creamy, sour, salty and a little sweet.
Ladle into bowls and top with cilantro. Eat around the lemongrass and galangal.
Spoon the thick cream from the top of the can into a wok or pot, about [[1 cup]], and heat over medium until it bubbles and the oil separates.
Add the curry paste and fry, stirring, until very fragrant.
Add the chicken and stir to coat in the paste, cooking for 3 minutes.
Pour in the remaining coconut milk and the stock. Simmer gently.
Add the eggplant and lime leaves and cook until the eggplant is tender and the chicken reaches 165°F (74°C).
Stir in the fish sauce and sugar. Taste for a balance of salty, sweet and spicy.
Fold in the basil and chili and turn off the heat.
Serve with steamed jasmine rice.
Heat the oil in a heavy pot and brown the beef in batches. Set aside.
Scoop the thick cream from the top of the coconut milk, about [[0.5 cup]], into the pot and cook until it splits and shines.
Add the curry paste and fry until fragrant, about 2 minutes.
Return the beef. Add the remaining coconut milk, [[1.5 cups]] water, cinnamon and bay leaves. Bring to a boil.
Cover and simmer on low until the beef is nearly tender.
Add the potatoes, onion and peanuts and simmer until the potatoes are soft.
Stir in the tamarind, fish sauce and sugar, then taste and adjust.
Remove the cinnamon and bay leaves and serve with jasmine rice.

ing: cut in short pieces, or green beans
st: Peel the papaya, cut out any seeds and shred the flesh with a julienne peeler or coarse grater.
In a large mortar, pound the garlic, chilies and dried shrimp to a rough paste.
Add the peanuts and pound lightly to crack them.
Add the long beans and bruise them gently with the pestle.
Add the sugar, fish sauce and lime juice, and stir until the sugar dissolves.
Add the papaya and tomatoes and pound and toss together, turning with a spoon, until the papaya softens slightly.
Taste and adjust to a balance of sour, salty, sweet and hot. Serve right away.
Rinse the rice, then cook it in [[1.5 cups]] water, covered, on low heat until tender, about 15 minutes. Keep warm.
Pound or chop the garlic and chilies together into a rough paste.
Mix the soy sauce, fish sauce, oyster sauce and sugar in a small cup.
Heat [[2 tbsp]] oil in a wok over high heat. Fry the garlic and chili paste for 20 seconds.
Add the pork and break it up. Stir-fry until fully cooked through (160°F/71°C) and slightly browned.
Pour in the sauce and toss for 30 seconds.
Add the basil, toss until just wilted, and turn off the heat.
Heat [[2 tbsp]] oil in a small pan and fry the eggs until the edges are crisp and the yolks still soft, or cook as you like. Serve the pork over rice, topped with an egg.
Heat [[1 tbsp]] oil in a pot, add the curry paste, curry powder and turmeric, and fry until fragrant.
Add about [[1 cup]] of the thick coconut milk and cook until it bubbles and the oil separates.
Add the chicken, the remaining coconut milk and the stock. Simmer partly covered until the chicken is cooked through and tender.
Stir in the fish sauce and sugar. Shred the chicken off the bone and return it to the pot.
Fry [[4 oz]] of the noodles in hot oil in a small pan until golden and crisp, about 1 minute. Drain on paper towels.
Boil the rest of the noodles according to the package, then drain.
Divide the boiled noodles among bowls and ladle the curry over them.
Top each bowl with crispy noodles, shallots, pickled greens and lime to squeeze over.

ing: raw, for the toasted rice powder
st: Toast the raw glutinous rice in a dry pan over medium heat, stirring, until deep golden and nutty.
Grind the toasted rice in a spice grinder or mortar into a coarse powder.
Cook the pork in a pan with [[0.25 cup]] water over medium heat, breaking it up, until no pink remains and it reaches 160°F (71°C).
Drain off excess liquid if needed and let the pork cool slightly.
Mix in the lime juice, fish sauce and chili flakes.
Stir in the shallots, green onions, mint, cilantro and [[2 tbsp]] of the toasted rice powder.
Taste and adjust the lime, fish sauce and chili.
Serve warm or at room temperature with lettuce leaves and sticky rice.
Rinse the rice until the water runs mostly clear, then soak in cold water.
Drain the rice and spread it in a steamer lined with cheesecloth or parchment with holes.
Steam over boiling water until the grains are translucent and tender.
Warm [[1 cup]] coconut milk, [[0.33 cup]] sugar and [[0.25 tsp]] salt in a pan until the sugar dissolves. Do not boil.
Mix the hot rice with the sweet coconut milk, cover, and rest until the rice has absorbed it.
For the sauce, heat [[0.5 cup]] coconut milk, the remaining sugar, the remaining salt and the cornstarch, stirring until slightly thick.
Slice the mango and arrange beside a scoop of rice.
Spoon the sauce over the rice and sprinkle with sesame seeds.
Wrap the shrimp paste in foil and toast it in a dry pan for 2 minutes per side until fragrant.
Roast the garlic, shallots and chilies in a dry pan, turning, until soft and charred in spots.
Peel the garlic and shallots.
Pound the chilies and garlic in a mortar to a coarse paste.
Add the shallots and toasted shrimp paste and pound until combined.
Stir in the fish sauce, sugar and lime juice. Taste for a balance of hot, salty, sour and sweet.
Spoon into a bowl and serve with fresh and blanched vegetables and sticky or jasmine rice.
Grind the peanuts in a food processor until finely crushed but still a little coarse.
Heat the oil in a saucepan over medium heat and fry the curry paste for 1 minute.
Pour in the coconut milk and stir until smooth and bubbling.
Add the ground peanuts, sugar, fish sauce, tamarind and water.
Simmer on low, stirring often, until thick and glossy with oil on top.
Taste and balance: sweet, salty and tangy. Add water if too thick.
Serve warm with grilled chicken satay or as a dip for vegetables.
Put the tea mix in a heat-safe pitcher and pour in [[2 cups]] boiling water.
Steep until strong and deep orange.
Strain through a fine strainer or cloth into another pitcher, pressing out the liquid.
Stir the sugar and condensed milk into the hot tea until dissolved.
Cool for a few minutes at room temperature.
Fill two tall glasses with ice and pour in the tea.
Float the evaporated milk on top and stir lightly before drinking.
Blend the rice flour, [[1 cup]] coconut milk, [[0.33 cup]] sugar, salt and cooked rice with [[0.25 cup]] water until smooth. Rest 20 minutes.
Whisk [[0.5 cup]] coconut milk with a pinch of salt for the creamy topping and set aside.
Heat a cast iron aebleskiver or mini pancake pan over medium heat and brush each well generously with oil.
Fill each well two thirds full with the base batter. Cover and cook 3 minutes until the edges are crisp and golden.
Spoon a teaspoon of the coconut topping into each, then add a few corn kernels or sliced scallion. Cover and cook 1 more minute.
Lift out with a small spoon and serve the same minute, while crisp outside and soft inside.
nt: Pan cooked, covered, on medium heat
Best swap: a nonstick mini muffin pan on the stove or a Danish aebleskiver pan if you have no khanom krok pan.

st: Mix the pork, shrimp, water chestnuts, cilantro roots, minced garlic, oyster sauce and white pepper. Knead for 2 minutes until sticky.
Place a heaping teaspoon of filling in the center of each wrapper. Gather the edges up around the filling and squeeze, leaving the top open.
Heat the oil over medium-low and fry the sliced garlic for 2 minutes until just golden. Remove with a slotted spoon.
Mix the black soy, vinegar and chili with [[1 tbsp]] water for the dip.
Steam the dumplings on an oiled plate or parchment over boiling water for 10 minutes. The pork must reach 160°F.
Top with crispy garlic and serve hot with the dip.
nt: Best swap: use ground chicken in place of the pork, same amount, and light soy sauce plus a pinch of sugar for oyster sauce.

st: Wash all the fruit under cold running water and scrub the rinds of the mango and pineapple. Pat dry with a clean towel so the cut surfaces stay crisp.
Peel the green mango and cut it into thick wedges, slicing down along the flat stone on each side. Keep each wedge about 1 cm thick so it holds up to the dip.
Trim the pineapple top and base, slice off the skin, and cut out the brown eyes in diagonal grooves. Quarter it lengthwise, remove the core, and slice into bite-size wedges.
Cut the watermelon into neat triangles or small rectangles, and slice the guava and rose apple into thin wedges. Drop them in ice water for 10 minutes to firm up, then drain well.
For the dip, stir [[2 tbsp]] sugar, [[1 tsp]] salt and [[1 tsp]] dried chili flakes in a small bowl with [[2 tbsp]] hot water until the sugar dissolves completely. Cool it.
Optional carving: use a small paring knife to cut a row of petals into a watermelon wedge or a pear half, working from the center outward, like a flower.
Fan the fruit on a cold platter in groups by color, keeping the sour mango and sweet pineapple apart. Place the dip bowl in the middle.
Serve right away with toothpicks, or chill up to 1 hour under plastic wrap. Dip the sour fruit into the salty-sweet-spicy mix.
nt: Best swap: green apple or underripe pear for the green mango, same wedge size, and add a squeeze of lime to the dip.

st: Pound the white peppercorns, garlic, cilantro roots and sliced lemongrass to a rough paste in a mortar, or blitz in a small food processor.
Stir the paste with [[3 tbsp]] fish sauce, [[1 tbsp]] oyster sauce and [[1 tbsp]] palm sugar. Rub it into the chicken and under the skin. Marinate in the fridge at least 1 hour, up to overnight.
Heat a grill for two zones: coals banked on one side. Bring the chicken to room temperature for 20 minutes while the fire heats.
Place the chicken skin side up on the cool side. Cover and cook 30 minutes at about 350°F, turning once, until the juices begin to run clear.
Move the chicken over the hot side and char for 3 to 5 minutes per side until deeply golden. The thickest piece must read 165°F.
Rest 5 minutes, chop into pieces and serve with the sweet chili sauce, sticky rice and papaya salad.
nt: Grilled over indirect then high direct charcoal heat
Best swap: roast on a rack at 425°F for 40 minutes, then broil 4 minutes. Use 3 tbsp chopped cilantro stems plus extra pepper for the roots.

st: Cut off the roots and dry tops from the lemongrass, peel the outer layer, and bash each stalk with the back of a knife to release the aroma. Cut into 2 inch pieces.
Bring [[6 cups]] water to a boil in a pot. Add the lemongrass and pandan leaves, reduce to a gentle simmer and cook 15 minutes.
Stir in [[0.5 cup]] sugar and the salt until dissolved, then turn off the heat and steep 5 minutes.
Strain into a pitcher, discarding the solids, and cool to room temperature.
Chill, then pour over plenty of ice and serve.
nt: Best swap: no pandan, skip it and add 1 tsp vanilla extract off the heat; lemongrass paste at 2 tbsp replaces fresh stalks in a pinch.

st: Pound the garlic, cilantro stems and white pepper in a mortar or mince finely to make a rough paste.
In a bowl, mix the paste with the coconut milk, oyster sauce, soy sauce and sugar. Add the pork and massage until every piece is coated.
Cover and marinate in the fridge for at least 1 hour, or up to overnight.
Thread the pork onto the soaked skewers in a loose accordion pattern so it cooks evenly.
Grill over medium-high heat or under a broiler, turning every 2 minutes, until browned with charred edges and cooked through to 160°F inside, about 8 minutes total.
Rest for 2 minutes and serve warm with sticky rice and a sweet chili dip if you like.
nt: Marinated, then grilled over medium-high heat
Best swap: pork neck is traditional, but boneless chicken thigh works 1 to 1; cook in a 450°F oven on a rack for 12 minutes if you have no grill.
